procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 09.06.2016 of the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, New Delhi in RP No. 526 of 2016
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The DCDRC allowed the complaint. The West Bengal State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (‘SCDRC’) set aside the order of the DCDRC. The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (the ‘NCDRC’) dismissed the revision petition preferred by the Appellant.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant approached the Supreme Court after the NCDRC dismissed their revision petition. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the orders of the NCDRC and SCDRC, and directed the Respondents to comply with the order of the DCDRC.

directions: The order of the NCDRC and the SCDRC are set aside.
The Respondents are directed to comply with the order of the DCDRC within one month from the date of this order.

issue.issue_text: Whether a report of the Medical Council is determinative in a case of medical negligence before a consumer forum, especially when it contradicts other evidentiary findings.

facts: A consumer complaint for medical negligence was filed after a 13-year-old boy lost vision following cataract surgery.
The District Forum found the doctors negligent and awarded compensation, relying on expert evidence that pointed to lapses in pre- and post-operative care.
However, the State Commission (SCDRC) and the National Commission (NCDRC) overturned this decision.
The SCDRC and NCDRC based their decisions exclusively on a report from the Medical Council which had exonerated the doctors of negligence.
law: While a report from the Medical Council is relevant evidence in a medical negligence case before a consumer forum, it is not determinative.
Consumer forums, particularly appellate bodies, have a duty to examine the evidence in its totality and cannot rely exclusively on a single report.
A Medical Council report cannot be the sole basis for a decision, especially when it contradicts other evidence on the record.
application: The Supreme Court found that the State and National Commissions erred by "mechanically and exclusively" relying on the Medical Council's report.
They failed in their duty to conduct a thorough examination of all the evidence, completely disregarding the uncontroverted expert testimony of another doctor.
This expert testimony had established a clear link between the lapses in post-operative care and the patient's subsequent loss of vision.
The Court noted that the Medical Council's report itself was not comprehensive, as it had not delved into the crucial nuances of pre-operative and post-operative care.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the Medical Council's report was determinative. It held that consumer forums must consider all evidence in totality. Because the State and National Commissions had ignored other significant evidence of negligence and relied solely on the Medical Council's report, their decisions were set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether an appellate consumer forum has a duty to examine the evidence on record in its totality, rather than exclusively relying on a single report.

facts: The case involved a medical negligence claim where the District Forum found in favor of the complainant, relying on expert evidence from a doctor (Dr. Gupta) that established a nexus between lapses in post-operative care and the patient's loss of vision.
The State Commission (SCDRC) and National Commission (NCDRC), however, overturned this decision.
The report from the Medical Council, which the appellate forums relied on, did not delve into the specific details of pre-operative and post-operative care.
law: An appellate consumer forum has a duty to examine the evidence on record in its totality.
While a report from the Medical Council can be relevant in determining a deficiency of service, it cannot be the sole determinative factor.
An appellate forum must undertake a more thorough examination of the evidence, especially when a Medical Council report contradicts other evidentiary findings made by a lower forum.
application: The Supreme Court found that both the State Commission and the National Commission failed in their duty to examine the evidence in totality.
Instead, they "mechanically and exclusively relied upon the Medical Council report" and reiterated its findings without any independent analysis or consideration of other evidence.
Specifically, they disregarded the uncontroverted expert evidence of Dr. Gupta and the specific findings of the District Forum regarding lapses in pre-operative and post-operative care.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the issue, holding that the appellate consumer forums (the State and National Commissions) had a duty to examine all the evidence and not just a single report. Their failure to consider the totality of the evidence, particularly the expert testimony and the District Forum's findings, was a failing that warranted setting aside their orders.

issue.issue_text: Whether the duty of care in cases of deficiency of medical services is limited to the surgery or extends to post-operative care.

facts: A 13-year-old boy lost vision in his right eye following a traumatic cataract surgery.
The District Forum found the doctor negligent due to lapses in both pre-operative and post-operative care, relying on uncontroverted expert testimony.
The State and National Commissions overturned this decision, relying solely on a Medical Council report that exonerated the doctor.
Expert evidence established a link between the lapses in post-operative care and the patient's subsequent loss of vision.
law: The Supreme Court affirmed the established legal principle that in cases of deficiency of medical services, a doctor's duty of care is not limited to the surgical procedure itself but extends to post-operative care.
application: The Court found that the doctor had failed in his post-operative duty of care.
Specific lapses were identified, including a significant delay in the follow-up review after the operation and a failure to address an abnormal vision rating recorded during a check-up.

The Court noted that the doctor himself admitted that managing a traumatic cataract in a child is difficult and prone to complications, which should have necessitated more diligent post-operative care, not less.
The Court relied on expert testimony that established a direct nexus between these post-operative failures and the patient's eventual loss of vision due to retinal detachment.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the duty of care in medical services extends to post-operative care. It held that the doctor's failure to provide adequate and timely follow-up after the surgery constituted a deficiency in service, which led to the patient's loss of vision. Therefore, the Court affirmed the finding of medical negligence.

issue.issue_text: Whether there was a deficiency in the medical services provided by the respondents, considering the lapses in both pre-operative and post-operative care for a traumatic cataract surgery.

facts: The case involved a traumatic cataract surgery on a child, which resulted in a complete loss of vision in the right eye.
The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (DCDRC) found specific lapses in both pre-operative and post-operative care by the respondent doctor.

An expert witness, Dr. Gupta, provided uncontroverted testimony establishing a nexus between the lapses in post-operative care and the patient's loss of vision. His evidence was not cross-examined, nor was contradictory evidence presented.
Specific lapses noted by Dr. Gupta included a failure to conduct a pre-operative drug allergy test, a significant delay in the post-operative review, and leaving an abnormal vision rating unchecked.
The State and National Commissions overturned the District forum's decision, relying exclusively on a Medical Council report that exonerated the doctors.
law: A doctor's duty of care in medical services does not end with the completion of a surgery but extends to post-operative care.
A report from the Medical Council, while relevant, is not determinative in a consumer forum case, especially when it contradicts other evidence on record.
Appellate forums, like the State and National Commissions, have a duty to examine the evidence in its totality rather than relying mechanically on a single report.
application: The Supreme Court found that the State and National Commissions erred by exclusively and mechanically relying on the Medical Council report while completely disregarding the other evidence, particularly the uncontroverted expert testimony of Dr. Gupta.
The Court gave significant weight to Dr. Gupta's testimony, which established a direct link between the doctor's failure in post-operative care and the patient's vision loss.

The Court noted that the respondent doctor's own admission that managing traumatic cataracts in children is difficult and prone to complications actually strengthened the finding of negligence, as it implied a higher standard of care was required, which was not met.
The Court concluded that the DCDRC's original findings were well-founded, as they were based on a thorough examination of the evidence, including the expert testimony.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted that there was a deficiency in the medical services provided. It affirmed the District forum's finding of negligence, holding that the uncontroverted expert evidence established clear lapses in post-operative care that led to the patient's loss of vision, and consequently set aside the orders of the State and National Commissions.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a report of the Medical Council is determinative in a case of medical negligence before a consumer forum, especially when it contradicts other evidentiary findings.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the lower consumer forums (NCDRC and SCDRC) erred by selectively appreciating evidence and completely disregarding other uncontroverted expert evidence, implying that the Medical Council report should not be the sole determinative factor.
respondent_arguments: The respondents argued that both the NCDRC and the SCDRC correctly placed reliance on the decision of the Medical Council to conclude there was an absence of negligence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an appellate consumer forum has a duty to examine the evidence on record in its totality, rather than exclusively relying on a single report.
appellant_arguments: The appellant contended that the NCDRC and SCDRC failed in their duty by undertaking a selective appreciation of evidence and ignoring expert testimony, instead of considering the evidence in its totality.
respondent_arguments: The respondents submitted that the forums' reliance on the Medical Council's report was correct, implying that this fulfilled their duty and a broader examination was unnecessary.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the duty of care in cases of deficiency of medical services is limited to the surgery or extends to post-operative care.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that there were significant lapses in the pre-operative and post-operative care provided by the respondents, which constituted negligence and a deficiency of service.
respondent_arguments: The text does not specify the respondents' direct argument on this point, but their reliance on the Medical Council report, which the court noted did not delve into pre-operative and post-operative care, suggests their defense focused on the surgery itself.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there was a deficiency in the medical services provided by the respondents, considering the lapses in both pre-operative and post-operative care for a traumatic cataract surgery.
appellant_arguments: The appellant contended that there was a clear deficiency in service due to the respondents' lapses in pre-operative and post-operative care, which was supported by uncontroverted expert evidence.
respondent_arguments: The respondents argued there was an absence of negligence, basing their conclusion on the Medical Council's report. They also noted that managing a traumatic cataract in a child is inherently difficult, unpredictable, and prone to complications.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In cases of deficiency of medical services, the duty of care does not end with the surgery.
obiter: The management and rehabilitation of traumatic cataract for a child is very difficult, unpredictable, and prone to complications.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court held that appellate consumer forums, such as the State and National Commissions, erred by mechanically and exclusively relying on a Medical Council report to overturn a finding of medical negligence. These forums have a duty to examine the evidence in its totality. The Court affirmed the District Forum's finding of deficiency in service, reasoning that the duty of care extends to post-operative standards, and that uncontroverted expert evidence had established a nexus between the respondents' lapses in post-operative care and the patient's subsequent loss of vision.
legal_tests_applied: A report of the Medical Council, while relevant, cannot be determinative in a consumer forum case for deficiency of service, especially when it contradicts other evidentiary findings.
An appellate forum has a duty to undertake a thorough examination of the evidence on record, rather than selectively relying on a single piece of evidence.
In cases of deficiency of medical services, the duty of care does not end with the surgery but extends to pre-operative and post-operative care.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant had lost before the State and National Commissions because those forums mechanically and exclusively relied upon the Medical Council report to conclude there was an absence of negligence, failing in their duty to examine the evidence in totality.
why_respondent_won: The respondent had won before the State and National Commissions because those forums incorrectly treated the Medical Council report as determinative, and consequently did not consider the specific, uncontroverted evidentiary findings made by the District Forum regarding lapses in post-operative care.
policy_considerations: Appellate forums are tasked with the duty of undertaking a more thorough examination of the evidence on record and cannot abdicate this judicial function by mechanically relying on an external body's report, which ensures a complete and fair adjudication of claims.
